section_summary: This section contains correspondence and State Department filing material on proposed exports to Japan of helium, helium-repurification equipment, and cartridge-priming machinery, together with inquiries about the Japanese arms industry. Its largest component is a 1937 Embassy despatch transmitting English translations of Japan’s Law for the Control of Firearms and Explosives and its detailed enforcement ordinance, covering licensing, manufacture, trade, possession, storage, transportation, inspection, and penalties. The section also includes telegrams summarizing Japanese arms-control law, internal routing and cross-reference sheets, and correspondence with a Michigan school principal.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence reply concerning helium sales and repurification equipment for Japan
subfiles.from: W. D. Puleston, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: James T. Howington, Vice President, the Helium Company
subfiles.about: The Navy informs the Helium Company that its request to quote helium and repurification equipment to a Japanese aeronautical institute has been referred to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: Puleston acknowledges Japanese interest in helium and helium-repurification equipment. He explains that the company’s request concerning the Institute of Aeronautical Policy in Tokyo has been sent to the State Department under interdepartmental procedure, with copies retained for Navy and State files.

subfiles.title: Helium Company request for Navy guidance on Japanese sales
subfiles.from: James T. Howington, Vice President, the Helium Company
subfiles.about: The company asks whether the Navy objects to its supplying helium-repurification plants and quoting helium prices to a Japanese institute.
subfiles.summary: The Institute of Aeronautical Policy in Tokyo requested prices for three repurification plants with capacities of 40,000, 4,500, and 3,000 cubic feet per hour. The company had also applied for an export permit for helium, reportedly intended for a commercial airship service, and sought the Navy’s views before disclosing specialized equipment information.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to the Secretary of the Navy concerning helium exports
subfiles.from: Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: The State Department acknowledges the Navy’s referral of the Helium Company proposal and encloses its reply to the company.
subfiles.summary: The letter records receipt of the Navy’s May 31 communication concerning proposed helium exports and information on repurification plants for Tokyo. It advises Swanson that a copy of the State Department’s response to the Helium Company is enclosed.

subfiles.title: State Department denial of the Helium Company’s proposed Japanese transaction
subfiles.from: Pierrepont Moffat, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The State Department explains that the Navy’s refusal to support helium exports prevents approval of the proposed sale to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of the Navy opposed the export of commercially produced helium for military-policy reasons and assumed that Japan would consequently have no need for repurification equipment. The State Department cites section 4 of the March 3, 1925 helium statute, under which presidential approval required joint recommendations from the Secretaries of War, Navy, and Interior. The Navy’s refusal therefore made approval impossible.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Saigon despatch on German chemical shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of State document file
subfiles.about: The sheet cross-references a Saigon despatch reporting German phosphate and chemical shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The filing note points to despatch no. 187 in file 782.94/50. Its subject annotation reports a freighter captain’s statement that North German Lloyd vessels traveling between Germany and Japan carried large quantities of phosphate and other chemicals for Japan.

subfiles.title: Telegram requesting information on Japanese arms and munitions legislation
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: The Department asks the Embassy for information on Japanese laws regulating or restricting the manufacture and export of arms and munitions.
subfiles.summary: This is the Department’s telegram no. 105, later identified in the Embassy’s reply. It requests a report on the principal provisions of Japanese arms-and-munitions controls.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram summarizing Japanese arms-control legislation
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo, signed Neville
subfiles.about: The Embassy summarizes the principal provisions of Japanese legislation governing arms and ammunition.
subfiles.summary: The telegram states that permits were required for manufacture, sale, import, and export, and that officials could cancel, suspend, or restrict permits for public-safety reasons. The government could restrict foreign trade for peace, military, or diplomatic reasons, while gunpowder and explosives manufacture was reserved to Japanese enterprises. Maximum penalties included two years’ imprisonment or a fine of one thousand yen, and permit rules left broad administrative discretion.

subfiles.title: Country list for regulations governing arms manufacture and export
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: The sheet lists countries for which information on arms-and-munitions manufacturing and export regulations was being assembled.
subfiles.summary: The country list includes Great Britain, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy, Germany, Czechoslovakia, the Soviet Union, Japan, Poland, Sweden, and Switzerland. A handwritten notation directs the material to Mr. Allen in room 305.

subfiles.title: Routing memorandum attaching the Tokyo arms-export telegram
subfiles.from: Division of Western European Affairs
subfiles.about: The memorandum routes a copy of the July 22, 1935 Tokyo telegram for information concerning the Soviet Union, Japan, and Poland.
subfiles.summary: The note identifies the attached telegram as dealing with the exportation of arms. It appears to form part of an internal comparative inquiry covering the Soviet Union, Japan, and Poland.

subfiles.title: File copy of Tokyo telegram no. 158 on Japanese arms-control law
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo, signed Neville
subfiles.about: This duplicate copy summarizes Japanese laws controlling the manufacture, trade, import, and export of arms and ammunition.
subfiles.summary: The telegram repeats that licensing applied to manufacturing, sales, imports, and exports and that permits could be canceled or restricted. It also notes restrictions based on public order, military needs, and foreign relations, the reservation of explosives manufacture to Japanese enterprises, criminal penalties, and extensive governmental discretion.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting copies and details of Japanese arms-control laws
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.to: American Chargé d’affaires ad interim, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department requests copies of Japanese arms-control legislation and full particulars of any import-licensing system.
subfiles.summary: Referring to Embassy telegram no. 158 of July 22, 1935, the Department asks for several copies of the cited law and other regulations concerning arms control. If Japan had established import licensing for arms, ammunition, and implements of war, the Embassy was to supply the list of covered articles and identify the authorities responsible for issuing licenses.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Commerce Department statement on munitions shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: Department of Commerce
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a Commerce Department letter containing an October statement of munitions shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference directs the reader to file 824.113/578. The referenced material was a Commerce Department statistical statement on munitions shipments to Japan during October.

subfiles.title: Flushing Public Schools inquiry about Japan’s arms industry
subfiles.from: Evart C. Scott, Principal, Flushing Public Schools
subfiles.about: Scott requests figures on governmental and private ownership in the Japanese arms industry for an imminent school use.
subfiles.summary: Scott asks what percentage of Japan’s arms industry was a government monopoly and which branches were privately owned. He requests an answer by December 16, the date on which the information was needed.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Evart C. Scott
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department states that its available material cannot answer Scott’s questions about ownership of the Japanese arms industry.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Scott’s December 9 request and its December 16 deadline. He regrets that the Department’s holdings do not contain the requested information and therefore cannot supply it.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2588 transmitting Japanese arms-control laws
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits translations of Japan’s basic firearms-and-explosives law and its enforcement regulations.
subfiles.summary: The despatch follows up the Embassy’s 1935 telegram summarizing Japanese arms-control legislation. Grew encloses translations of the principal statute and ordinance but notes that regulations on governmental sales, explosives storage, Taiwan, Karafuto, the Kwantung Leased Territory, and other areas outside Japan proper were not translated. Copies were routed to the Office of Naval Intelligence and Military Intelligence Division.

subfiles.title: Law for the Control of Firearms and Explosives
subfiles.from: Government of Japan; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The translated statute establishes Japan’s basic legal controls over firearms, ammunition, gunpowder, and explosives.
subfiles.summary: Law No. 53 of April 13, 1910, as amended in 1917 and 1922, requires permits for manufacture, repair, sale, import, and export and restricts explosives manufacture to Japanese-controlled enterprises. It authorizes inspections, safety orders, trade and transportation restrictions, provisional detention, and detailed implementing ordinances. Violations could bring imprisonment, penal servitude, fines, confiscation, and liability for acts committed by employees or household members. The law took effect on May 1, 1911, with a further 1922 amendment effective May 1, 1923.

subfiles.title: Regulations for Enforcement of the Law for the Control of Firearms and Explosives
subfiles.from: Government of Japan; translated by the American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The ordinance supplies detailed administrative, commercial, storage, transportation, and safety rules implementing Japan’s firearms-and-explosives law.
subfiles.summary: Imperial Ordinance No. 16 defines firearms, powders, explosives, and explosive manufactures and specifies exemptions for experiments, hunting, pest control, schools, and rifle ranges. It establishes licensing authorities, dealer classes, transaction limits, possession rules, import and export procedures, magazine requirements, maximum storage quantities, safety distances, and controls on blasting and concealed weapons. It also regulates minors, transportation, testing and disposal of defective explosives, and ministerial responsibility for rail, postal, maritime, factory, and storage rules. Penalties include imprisonment, penal servitude, detention, and fines; amendments were made in 1917 and 1923.

subfiles.title: File jacket for Waterbury Farrel Foundry and Machine Company case
subfiles.from: Department of State filing office
subfiles.about: The jacket identifies the case concerning the Waterbury Farrel company’s proposed sale of arms-related machinery to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The jacket labels the subject as the sale of arms and munitions to Japan by the Waterbury Farrel Foundry and Machine Company. It bears the date March 28, 1932, and standard instructions not to remove, rearrange, stamp, or deface the enclosed papers.

subfiles.title: Waterbury Farrel inquiry about exporting a cartridge-priming machine to Japan
subfiles.from: Z. P. Candee, Waterbury Farrel Foundry and Machine Company
subfiles.about: The company asks whether an embargo prevents export to Japan of a machine used to prime cartridges.
subfiles.summary: Waterbury Farrel states that it had manufactured similar machinery for Frankford Arsenal and had received a Japanese inquiry for one machine. The War Department had already indicated that it had no objection to the export. The company asks the State Department whether any applicable embargo remained in force.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on export of cartridge-priming machinery
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Waterbury Farrel Foundry and Machine Company
subfiles.about: The Department advises that no embargo applies to the proposed shipment of a cartridge-priming machine to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges the company’s March 28 inquiry. He states that there was no embargo applicable to the described shipment to Japan.
